title: Ang 728–729: Suhi begins
hookLine: Guru Nanak opens the raga of union
tomorrow: if someone guards your head, can anything still go wrong?

lines: A DARK RING ON YOUR FINGER.
BRIGHT BRONZE, BLACK ON THE HAND.
WHY START A RAGA OF UNION HERE?
cards: Cheap jewelry looks great under store lights. A week later, there's a dark ring on your finger. Suhi, the raga of union, begins on ang 728, and a page later Guru Nanak points at something shiny.
In paraphrase: bronze is bright and gleaming, but rub it, and its blackness comes off on your hand; wash it again and again, and it's still not clean.
So here's the puzzle: why would a raga of union start by rubbing black off bronze?

teach.b: Tradition tells the story behind it. Guru Nanak and his companion Mardana stopped at a rest-house kept by a man called Sajjan, a name that means friend.

It looked like a welcoming place on the road, tradition says, with a place to pray for Hindus and a place for Muslims. At night, Sajjan robbed his guests, and worse. When the Guru's turn came, he sang.
Bright bronze that leaves black on your hand.

teach.h: FRIENDS WALK WITH YOU ALL THE WAY.
teach.b: And then, in paraphrase, the line that turned the story: those are my friends, my sajjan, who go along with me, and who stand with me where the account is called.
Tradition says Sajjan heard his own name in the hymn, fell at the Guru's feet, and changed his life. So, the puzzle.
Union in Suhi doesn't start with shine. A surface can look welcoming and still leave a mark. The bride songs of this raga come later; Guru Nanak begins with what makes a friend a friend.
Not the gleam, but the one who walks with you all the way, to where the account is asked. Union.

how: Sikhs tell the Janamsakhi story of Guru Nanak and Sajjan, and the Suhi hymn on ang 729, with its line about friends who walk with you, is sung in kirtan.

o: where Suhi begins, the raga of union
where the Lavan, the wedding rounds, are

p: rub it, and black comes off
walk with you to the reckoning
the Guru's companion on the road

s: Suhi, the raga of union, is only about marriage
it opens with what makes a friend a friend; the bride songs come later.
in the hymn, the shiny bronze is a picture of true goodness
rub it and the black comes off on your hand: shine isn't goodness.
tradition says Sajjan's rest-house looked welcoming from outside
with a place to pray for Hindus and for Muslims, while he robbed his guests at night.

games.q: your new friend group is fun and always posting together. your old friend is quieter, but shows up every time things go wrong. her recital is the same night as their party. what fits ang 729?
o: go to the recital; a friend is the one who walks with you.
go to the party; new friendships need more effort early on.
skip both so nobody feels you chose one over the other.
games.why: Guru Nanak's test isn't the shine: friends are the ones who go along with you and stand with you where the account is asked.

practice: Stand and walk slowly, in the room or a hallway, letting the breath set the pace. Every few steps, bring to mind one person who has walked with you when it counted.
If walking isn't easy right now, rest your hands on your knees and walk the route in your mind.

wordCard.voice: Ang 728. Where Suhi begins, the raga of union, and a page on, Guru Nanak's friend who walks with you all the way.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: sajan, friend; those are friends who walk along with me (ang 729).

carryVoice: Union: the shine doesn't make the friend; the walking does. Day fifteen thirty-five, side by side.
